content: Hexokinase 3 (HK3) is an enzyme encoded by the HK3 gene located on chromosome 5 in humans. This enzyme belongs to the hexokinase family, which catalyzes the phosphorylation of glucose to produce glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), a critical first step in most glucose metabolism pathways. Like other hexokinases, HK3 is an allosteric enzyme that is inhibited by its product, G6P. Structurally, HK3 is one of four highly homologous hexokinase isoforms found in mammalian cells. It has a molecular weight of approximately 100 kDa and consists of two similar 50-kDa domains located at its N-terminal and C-terminal regions. This structural similarity, along with the existence of a 50-kDa hexokinase (HK4), suggests that the 100-kDa hexokinases likely evolved from a 50-kDa precursor through gene duplication and tandem ligation. Similar to HK1, only the C-terminal domain of HK3 exhibits catalytic activity, while the N-terminal domain is predicted to contain binding sites for glucose and G6P, as well as a 32-residue region essential for proper protein folding. The catalytic activity of HK3 depends on the interaction between its two terminal domains. Unlike HK1 and HK2, HK3 lacks a mitochondrial binding sequence at its N-terminal region. Functionally, HK3 is a cytoplasmic isoform of hexokinase and a member of the sugar kinase family. It catalyzes the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of glucose to G6P, which is the rate-limiting and first obligatory step in glucose metabolism. Physiological levels of G6P regulate this process by inhibiting HK3 through negative feedback, although inorganic phosphate can relieve this inhibition. Inorganic phosphate can also directly regulate HK3, and this dual regulation may better suit its anabolic functions. By phosphorylating glucose, HK3 effectively traps glucose within the cell, committing it to energy metabolism. Compared to HK1 and HK2, HK3 has a higher affinity for glucose and can bind the substrate even at physiological levels, although this binding may be attenuated by intracellular ATP. Uniquely, HK3 can be inhibited by high concentrations of glucose and is less sensitive to G6P inhibition. Despite its lack of mitochondrial association, HK3 also plays a role in protecting cells against apoptosis. Overexpression of HK3 has been shown to increase ATP levels, reduce reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, attenuate reductions in mitochondrial membrane potential, and enhance mitochondrial biogenesis. Overall, HK3 may promote cell survival by controlling ROS levels and boosting energy production. HK3 expression is inducible under hypoxic conditions via a hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-dependent pathway. This inducible expression suggests an adaptive role for HK3 in metabolic responses to changes in the cellular environment. HK3 is ubiquitously expressed in tissues, albeit at relatively low levels, with higher abundance reported in lung, kidney, and liver tissues. Within cells, HK3 localizes to the cytoplasm and is thought to bind the perinuclear envelope. It is the predominant hexokinase in myeloid cells, particularly granulocytes. Clinically, HK3 is overexpressed in malignant follicular thyroid nodules. In combination with cyclin A and galectin-3, HK3 could serve as a diagnostic biomarker for screening malignancy in patients. Conversely, HK3 expression is repressed in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) blast cells and acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) patients. It has been proposed that HK3 transcription may be directly activated during neutrophil differentiation to support the short-term survival of mature neutrophils. Regulators such as PML-RARA and CEBPA repress HK3 expression in AML. In acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), functional enrichment analysis has identified HK3 as a key gene, suggesting that it shares anti-apoptotic functions with HK1 and HK2.
